--- title: DataLoaders author: Marie-Hélène Burle mermaid: theme: neutral --- :::{.def} Datasets hand out one sample at a time, but models consume batches of tensors. The [DataLoader](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html#torch.utils.data.DataLoader) bridges the two: it shuffles the data, groups it into batches, and loads those batches in parallel worker processes. This page covers the options that matter and how to diagnose a run in which the accelerator waits for data. ::: ## Packages ::: {#7c7f4f31 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import time # to time experiments import torch from matplotlib import pyplot as plt # to look at a batch from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Subset from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT from torchvision.transforms import v2 as T ``` ::: - `torch.utils.data` provides the DataLoader machinery. - `torchvision.transforms` (its modern `v2` API, imported as `T` by convention) lets us turn images into tensors. ## Dataset with transform We need to reload the EuroSAT data and we need to turn our PIL images into tensors because this what the whole PyTorch machinery (DataLoaders, training, etc.) expects. For this, we create a transform with [torchvision transforms v2](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/transforms.html): ::: {#ec9be82b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} to_tensor = T.Compose([T.ToImage(), T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True)]) ``` ::: - [`T.ToImage()`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.ToImage.html) turns the PIL image into a [uint8]{.codelike} tensor of shape `(channels, height, width)`. - [`T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True)`](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/generated/torchvision.transforms.v2.ToDtype.html) converts it to [float32]{.codelike} and rescales the values from the 0-255 range into `[0, 1]`. - `T.Compose` chains the two. This minimal pair is all we need to obtain batches; the full preprocessing pipeline (with normalization and augmentation) is the topic of the [next section of the course](pt2_augmentation.qmd). We store that transform as an attribute to the dataset: ::: {#4ea6bb4b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} eurosat = EuroSAT(root="data", transform=to_tensor) eurosat.transform ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` Compose( ToImage() ToDtype(scale=True) ) ``` ::: ::: :::{.note} Transforms are applied on-the-fly inside the dataset's `__getitem__()` method when an item is indexed or fetched by a DataLoader. ::: Then we need to restore the split saved [in the previous section](pt2_datasets.qmd), so that every section of the course evaluates on the same validation set: ::: {#99c4cfef .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} idx = torch.load("data/split.pt", weights_only=True) train = Subset(eurosat, idx["train"]) val = Subset(eurosat, idx["val"]) print(f"{len(train)} training examples and {len(val)} validation examples") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 21600 training examples and 5400 validation examples ``` ::: ::: ## From samples to batches A dataset or Subset can be indexed to return one sample at a time (here an image tensor and its label): ::: {#368dd772 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} img, label = train[0] print(f"First image:\n{img}\nFirst label:\n{label}") print(f"Shape of the image tensor: {img.shape}") print(f"{img.min().item():.2f} {img.max().item():.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` First image: Image([[[0.2353, 0.2353, 0.2392, ..., 0.1882, 0.1843, 0.1843], [0.2392, 0.2392, 0.2392, ..., 0.1882, 0.1843, 0.1843], [0.2392, 0.2353, 0.2353, ..., 0.2000, 0.1843, 0.1922], ..., [0.2902, 0.2902, 0.2902, ..., 0.2510, 0.2510, 0.2471], [0.2824, 0.2863, 0.2667, ..., 0.2667, 0.2588, 0.2510], [0.2392, 0.2392, 0.2392, ..., 0.2588, 0.2549, 0.2510]], [[0.3020, 0.3020, 0.2980, ..., 0.3059, 0.3020, 0.3020], [0.2980, 0.2980, 0.2980, ..., 0.3059, 0.3020, 0.3020], [0.2941, 0.2941, 0.2941, ..., 0.3059, 0.2902, 0.2980], ..., [0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333, ..., 0.3098, 0.3098, 0.3059], [0.3373, 0.3412, 0.3176, ..., 0.3255, 0.3176, 0.3098], [0.2980, 0.2980, 0.2902, ..., 0.3176, 0.3137, 0.3098]], [[0.4196, 0.4196, 0.4275, ..., 0.4157, 0.4118, 0.4118], [0.4196, 0.4196, 0.4275, ..., 0.4157, 0.4118, 0.4118], [0.4078, 0.4157, 0.4235, ..., 0.4118, 0.4039, 0.4118], ..., [0.4431, 0.4431, 0.4510, ..., 0.4235, 0.4235, 0.4196], [0.4510, 0.4549, 0.4431, ..., 0.4392, 0.4392, 0.4314], [0.4118, 0.4118, 0.4157, ..., 0.4314, 0.4353, 0.4314]]], ) First label: 1 Shape of the image tensor: torch.Size([3, 64, 64]) 0.17 0.46 ``` ::: ::: :::{.note} The image is now a PyTorch image tensor and the pixel values are in `[0, 1]`. ::: A DataLoader takes care of grouping samples into batches. ::: {#d4b73eb7 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=64) ``` ::: The loader calls `__getitem__()` repeatedly, then stacks the samples of each batch into tensors with its collate function. ::: {#af1aa89e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} images, labels = next(iter(loader)) print(images.shape, images.dtype) print(labels.shape, labels.dtype) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` torch.Size([64, 3, 64, 64]) torch.float32 torch.Size([64]) torch.int64 ``` ::: ::: One batch is a pair of tensors: - `images` stacks 64 images of 3 colour channels and 64 × 64 pixels as one [float32]{.codelike} tensor. - `labels` holds the 64 class indices as one integer tensor. A loader over the training set yields 338 batches: ::: {#bebd4023 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(len(DataLoader(train, batch_size=64))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 338 ``` ::: ::: 21,600 images in batches of 64 gives 337.5, rounded up to 338: the last batch is incomplete (32 images). `drop_last=True` drops it instead, giving 337 uniform batches. This is sometimes done for training (uniform batch statistics), never for evaluation (every sample must be counted). :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How to choose the batch size? The batch size is a crucial hyperparameter: it impacts your training speed, model stability, and final accuracy. ### Default strategy If you are unsure where to start, **use a batch size of 32**. 32 is small enough to provide a regularizing effect (helping the model generalize) but large enough to benefit from parallel processing on GPUs. ### Standard values Always use powers of 2 (32, 64, 128, 256) because GPUs and CPUs are optimized for binary operations, and this aligns memory allocation efficiently. | | **Small batch size** | **Large batch size** | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Training speed** | Slower: less efficient use of GPU | Faster: maximizes GPU throughput | | **Generalization** | Better: the "noise" in the gradient helps the model escape sharp local minima | Worse: can lead to overfitting | | **Convergence** | Noisy training curve: loss fluctuates | Smoother training curve: stable descent | | **Memory usage** | Low: good for limited VRAM | High: risk of OOM | ### Tuning the batch size #### Ceiling Your maximum batch size is dictated by your GPU memory (VRAM). If you hit an [out of memory (OOM) error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_memory), you need to back down to the previous successful power of 2 (this is your hardware maximum). #### Performance Just because you *can* fit a batch size of 4096 doesn't mean you *should*. If training is stable but slow, double to 64, then double again to 128. You can increase the batch size to the hardware maximum to speed up epochs. If the model overfits or diverges, try reducing the batch size. The "noisy" updates act like regularization, preventing the model from memorizing the data too perfectly. ### Advanced techniques - **Gradient accumulation:** If you need a batch size of 64 for stability but your GPU only fits 16, you can use *gradient accumulation*. You process 4 mini-batches of 16, accumulate the gradients, and update the weights once. This mathematically simulates a batch size of 64. - **Dynamic batching:** Some advanced training regimes start with a small batch size to stabilize early training and increase it over time to speed up convergence (similar to learning rate decay). ### Learning rate If you change your batch size significantly, you should adjust your learning rate. A rule that works well until you get to very large batch sizes is to double the learning rate when you double the batch size. ::: ::::{.exo} :::{.yourturn} Your turn: ::: - How many batches does `DataLoader(val, batch_size=128)` produce? (Predict first, then check). - How many batches does `DataLoader(val, batch_size=128, drop_last=True)` produce? (Predict first, then check). - How large is the last batch? :::: ## Shuffling Should you shuffle the data? As seen [in the previous section](pt2_datasets.qmd), EuroSAT files are stored class by class (`AnnualCrop` first, then `Forest`, etc.). Without shuffling, a loader feeds batches of a single class: ::: {#9be97aa9 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} plain = EuroSAT(root="data", transform=to_tensor) print(next(iter(DataLoader(plain, batch_size=8)))[1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tensor([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]) ``` ::: ::: Our training set does not have this problem: the indices drawn by `random_split` are already shuffled, so batches are mixed. But without `shuffle=True`, the iteration follows the same fixed order at every epoch: ::: {#219e41d0 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} a = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8)))[1] b = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8)))[1] print(a) print(b) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tensor([1, 0, 0, 7, 6, 6, 4, 2]) tensor([1, 0, 0, 7, 6, 6, 4, 2]) ``` ::: ::: With `shuffle=True`, a fresh order is drawn at every epoch: ::: {#f7d9d81a .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} a = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8, shuffle=True)))[1] b = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8, shuffle=True)))[1] print(a) print(b) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tensor([1, 8, 2, 5, 1, 0, 7, 6]) tensor([1, 0, 0, 7, 4, 6, 4, 3]) ``` ::: ::: Shuffling can be made reproducible by seeding a generator: ::: {#29339f82 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} g1 = torch.Generator().manual_seed(42) g2 = torch.Generator().manual_seed(42) a = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8, shuffle=True, generator=g1)))[1] b = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8, shuffle=True, generator=g2)))[1] print(torch.equal(a, b)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` True ``` ::: ::: :::{.notenoit} - Note that a `torch.Generator` is a stateful stream of random numbers. The iteration moves the cursor in that stream: ::: {#e4516483 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(42) a = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8, shuffle=True, generator=g)))[1] b = next(iter(DataLoader(train, batch_size=8, shuffle=True, generator=g)))[1] print(torch.equal(a, b)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` False ``` ::: ::: - The generator also seeds the random draws happening inside worker processes, which will matter once we add random augmentation in the next section. - Shuffle the training data only: validation must be deterministic and its order is irrelevant. ::: Here is one shuffled batch: ::: {#43979bbe .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=64, shuffle=True) images, labels = next(iter(loader)) fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(10.2, 5.5)) for ax, image, lbl in zip(axes.flat, images[:8], labels[:8]): ax.imshow(image.permute(1, 2, 0)) # CHW -> HWC for matplotlib ax.set_title(eurosat.classes[lbl], fontsize=9) ax.axis("off") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](pt2_dataloaders_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=778 height=423} ::: :::
Mixed classes within each batch give gradient estimates that are not dominated by one class at a time. ## Loading in parallel Decoding and transforming images is CPU work. With the default `num_workers=0`, it all happens in the main Python process, one image at a time. While the main process decodes the next batch, the accelerator has nothing to do. With `num_workers=n`, the DataLoader spawns n worker processes. Each worker prepares whole batches (decode, transform, collate) and pushes them into a queue, from which the main process pulls as it consumes them: ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false flowchart LR classDef default color:#0081c2, stroke:#0081c2; D[(files on disk)] --> w1 & w2 & w3 subgraph W [worker processes] w1[decode + transform] --> b1[batch] w2[decode + transform] --> b2[batch] w3[decode + transform] --> b3[batch] end b1 & b2 & b3 --> Q[prefetch queue] Q --> P[pinned memory] -->|async copy| G([training step on the accelerator]) ``` The queue smooths out the hiccups: workers run ahead of the consumer (by how much is the `prefetch_factor` option seen below), so loading overlaps with compute. Let's measure. The function below runs one warmup pass (spawning workers and paying the one-time startup cost), then times a second pass at steady state: ::: {#a0173de5 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} def timed_pass(num_workers): """Time one full pass over the training data at steady state.""" loader = DataLoader( train, batch_size=64, num_workers=num_workers, persistent_workers=num_workers > 0, # keeps workers alive: next section ) for _ in loader: pass # warmup t0 = time.perf_counter() n = 0 for _, labels in loader: n += labels.numel() dt = time.perf_counter() - t0 del loader # shuts the workers down assert n == len(train) return dt ``` ::: ::: {#53f57c0e .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} for w in (0, 2, 4, 8): print(f"num_workers={w}: {timed_pass(w):5.1f} s") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` num_workers=0: 6.4 s num_workers=2: 3.8 s num_workers=4: 2.0 s num_workers=8: 1.2 s ``` ::: ::: On this machine (16 CPU threads), one pass over the 21,600 training images takes about 8.5 s in the main process, and about 1.7 s with 8 workers. The gains flatten past 4 workers: at that point decoding is no longer the bottleneck. How many workers should you use? - `num_workers` counts per DataLoader: the training and validation loaders each spawn their own set. - Every worker is a separate process with a copy of the dataset object and its prefetch buffers: more workers, more RAM. Numbers beyond your CPU count are wasted. - 4 is a reasonable default. Measure on your machine, as we just did. ## Worker lifetime Workers are spawned when iteration starts and die when the iterator is exhausted, so a fresh set is spawned at every epoch. `persistent_workers=True` (used in the timings above) keeps them alive across epochs. To see why this matters, let's time two passes without it: ::: {#00abd636 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=64, num_workers=2) for _ in range(2): t0 = time.perf_counter() n = 0 for _, labels in loader: n += labels.numel() print(f"pass: {time.perf_counter() - t0:5.1f} s") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pass: 7.9 s pass: 7.8 s ``` ::: ::: Each pass took around 11 s on this machine: slower than loading with no workers at all (8.5 s). What happened? Python 3.14 changed the default multiprocessing start method on Linux from `fork` to `forkserver`. A fresh worker no longer inherits the parent process with its libraries already imported: it starts from the forkserver's pristine interpreter and must import torch before it can decode anything. Every pass re-spawned workers and re-paid those imports. With `persistent_workers=True`, the startup is paid once: ::: {#c264905f .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=64, num_workers=4, persistent_workers=True) for _ in range(3): t0 = time.perf_counter() n = 0 for _, labels in loader: n += labels.numel() print(f"pass: {time.perf_counter() - t0:5.1f} s") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pass: 9.9 s pass: 2.0 s pass: 2.0 s ``` ::: ::: The first pass pays the worker startup (about 15 s), then each full pass takes about 2.7 s. The trade-off: idle workers hold RAM between epochs, and the data must not change behind their back. For training loops, this option is almost always worth it. :::{.notenoit} In a Python script, the same forkserver default has another consequence: code that creates DataLoaders with workers must sit under the main guard ```python if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` Without it, worker startup re-imports your script: module-level code runs again (our draft script printed all of its output twice) and the run crashes with a `RuntimeError`. Notebook cells are immune: an interactive `__main__` cannot be re-imported. We will need this guard again for the training scripts of the cluster section. ::: ## Prefetching Each worker prepares `prefetch_factor` batches (2 by default) ahead of the one being consumed, so up to `num_workers × prefetch_factor` batches sit in the queue. With fast storage and cheap transforms the default is plenty. Raise it when the storage is slow (e.g. a network filesystem) or the transforms are expensive, so that occasional slow reads get absorbed by the queue rather than stalling the accelerator. It costs buffer RAM and only takes effect with `num_workers > 0`: ```{.python} loader = DataLoader( train, batch_size=64, num_workers=4, prefetch_factor=4, ) ``` ## Pinned memory By default, tensors loaded in the main process live in pageable memory, which the operating system can move or swap out to disk. Transfers to the accelerator from *pinned* (page-locked) memory are faster and can run asynchronously (with `.to(device, non_blocking=True)`) while the previous training step computes. With `pin_memory=True`, the DataLoader copies each batch into pinned memory for you. Measured on our GPU for our batch shape (64, 3, 64, 64) float32 (3 MiB) and for a batch 8 times larger (24 MiB), one host-to-device copy: ``` batch 64: pageable 541 µs pinned 495 µs batch 512: pageable 6250 µs pinned 3933 µs ``` A few percent at our batch size and about 40% for the larger one: small, but free. The caveat is that pinned memory cannot be swapped: pin batches, not datasets. ## Data loading bottleneck How do you diagnose an accelerator-starved run? The classic symptom is an accelerator that alternates between busy and idle: watch the GPU-Util column of `nvidia-smi` while training (see our [GPU notes](../gpu_intro.qmd)) or check epoch times against a rough estimate of pure compute. We trained a small CNN (about 95,000 parameters) on EuroSAT for two epochs per configuration on a laptop GPU (RTX 2060, 6 GiB): ```{.python} for num_workers in (0, 2, 4, 8): loader = DataLoader( train, batch_size=64, shuffle=True, pin_memory=True, num_workers=num_workers, persistent_workers=num_workers > 0, ) for epoch in range(2): # warmup, then the timed epoch t0 = time.perf_counter() for x, y in loader: x = x.to(device, non_blocking=True) y = y.to(device, non_blocking=True) loss = loss_fn(model(x), y) optimizer.zero_grad() loss.backward() optimizer.step() if epoch: # mean_util: average of the nvidia-smi samples print(f"num_workers={num_workers}: " f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:5.1f} s/epoch, GPU util {mean_util:3.0f}%") ``` We sampled utilization with [`nvidia-smi`](../../python/gpu_clusters.qmd#logging-metrics) in a background thread and got the following results: ``` num_workers=0: 10.7 s/epoch, GPU util 31% num_workers=2: 5.2 s/epoch, GPU util 51% num_workers=4: 3.2 s/epoch, GPU util 85% num_workers=8: 3.1 s/epoch, GPU util 89% ``` These numbers show that: - With loading in the main process, the GPU did useful work 31% of the time: the rest was waiting for JPEG decoding. A pure loading pass took 8.1 s—longer than a compute-bound epoch. - Four workers hid loading under compute: epochs got 3.4× faster and utilization reached 85%. - The eighth worker bought almost nothing: with this model, 4 workers already feed the GPU as fast as it consumes. These ratios are specific to a small model on a laptop GPU. A larger model computes longer per batch, so it needs fewer workers to stay busy. When a run is accelerator-starved, tune in this order: more workers first, then `prefetch_factor`, then `pin_memory`. ## Our loaders Here are the loaders that we will use for the rest of the course: ::: {#a0a4719d .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} loader_kwargs = { "batch_size": 64, "num_workers": 4, "persistent_workers": True, "pin_memory": torch.accelerator.is_available(), } train_loader = DataLoader(train, shuffle=True, **loader_kwargs) val_loader = DataLoader(val, **loader_kwargs) print(len(train_loader), len(val_loader)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 338 85 ``` ::: ::: - Batches of 64: a good size for the small models of this course. - Four persistent workers each, as measured above. - Pinned memory when an accelerator is present. - Shuffling for training only. Batches of [float32]{.codelike} tensors in `[0, 1]` now flow from both splits. The transform that made this happen was minimal; the [next section](pt2_augmentation.qmd) gives it its full treatment: normalization and augmentation.
